semantic_correction.stem: A client who smokes daily is scheduled for elective surgery in 6 weeks and asks whether quitting now would matter. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.A: Yes. Quitting now and remaining smoke-free through recovery can reduce wound and breathing complications after surgery.
options.B: Smoking affects long-term health but has little relationship to wound healing or respiratory complications after surgery.
options.C: Continue smoking until after surgery because stopping during the weeks before an operation can increase perioperative complications.
options.D: Preoperative smoking cessation is mainly useful for clients with diagnosed chronic lung disease rather than other surgical patients.

semantic_correction.rationale: The American College of Surgeons states that smoking increases the risk of problems during and after surgery, including breathing and wound-healing complications. ACS patient guidance specifically advises quitting 4 to 6 weeks before an operation and remaining smoke-free after surgery; this can substantially reduce wound complications. Because this elective procedure is 6 weeks away, stopping now is clinically meaningful and should be encouraged.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach that preoperative smoking cessation reduces perioperative risk and should be encouraged before elective surgery and during recovery.
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Quit Smoking before Your Operation; Preparing for Your Operation
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Current ACS surgical-patient education guidance accessed August 21, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Quit Smoking before Surgery — smoking increases problems during/after surgery; quitting 4–6 weeks before the operation and staying smoke-free 4 weeks afterward can decrease wound complications. Preparing for Your Operation — smoking increases breathing and wound-healing problems; quitting at least 4 weeks before surgery and remaining smoke-free can decrease risk
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: ACS advises preoperative smoking cessation because smoking raises respiratory and wound-healing risk; quitting several weeks before surgery and remaining smoke-free through recovery reduces complications.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the 'only chronic lung disease' absolute cue, shortened the uniquely long correct answer, and retained ACS's 4–6-week preoperative cessation and postoperative smoke-free guidance without overstating a universal exact duration requirement.

audit_findings_append.source_locator: Quit Smoking before Your Operation and Preparing for Your Operation
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — perioperative risk reduction
audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item correctly teaches that quitting 6 weeks before elective surgery is clinically beneficial for reducing wound and respiratory risk.

option_audit.A: Correct. It matches ACS guidance on preoperative cessation and reduced wound/respiratory risk.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Smoking is directly associated with perioperative respiratory and wound-healing complications.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. ACS recommends cessation before surgery rather than continuing smoking until afterward.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Surgical smoking-cessation benefit is not restricted to clients with chronic lung disease.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone accurately applies current ACS guidance to the 6-week preoperative window in the stem.
cueing_check: All four options are perioperative smoking-counseling statements of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
